# Object Conversions
<!-- Slide 28 -->

## Can One Class Become Another? {.smaller}

- `Fahrenheit report = today;`

::: notes
Slides 29–37

Fahrenheit is a new class that stores degrees Fahrenheit. today is still the Celsius Temperature.
:::

<!-- Slide 29 -->

---

## Two Places to Put the Conversion

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%" style="font-size: 50%;"}
**In the target: a converting constructor**

~~~cpp
class Fahrenheit {
private:
    double degrees;

public:
    // Built from a Temperature
    Fahrenheit(const Temperature& t);
};
~~~
:::

::: {.column width="50%" style="font-size: 50%;"}
**In the source: a conversion operator**

~~~cpp
class Temperature {
private:
    double celsius;

public:
    // Becomes a Fahrenheit
    operator Fahrenheit() const;
};
~~~
:::

::::

::: notes
Both make Fahrenheit report = today; compile. The next slide decides between them.
:::

<!-- Slide 30 -->

---

## Which One to Write?

| | Converting constructor | Conversion operator |
|---|---|---|
| Lives in | `Fahrenheit`, the target | `Temperature`, the source |
| You must be able to edit | The target class | The source class |

- Write both and the compiler may reject `Fahrenheit report = today;` as ambiguous, or quietly pick one.
- Write one, in the class you own. When you own both, prefer the constructor: the class being built controls how it is built.

::: notes
Tested with g++: with only the two conversions, g++ reports the conversion as ambiguous. Add Temperature's operator double and the same line compiles with no warning and uses the constructor. Either way, the author no longer controls which conversion runs.
:::

<!-- Slide 31 -->

---

## Temperature to Fahrenheit

::: {style="font-size: 70%;"}
~~~cpp
class Temperature {
private:
    double celsius;

public:
    Temperature(double value = 0.0) { celsius = value; }
    operator double() const { return celsius; }
};

class Fahrenheit {
private:
    double degrees;

public:
    Fahrenheit(double value = 32.0) { degrees = value; }

    // Converts a Celsius Temperature to Fahrenheit
    Fahrenheit(const Temperature& t) { degrees = t * 9.0 / 5.0 + 32.0; }

    double value() const { return degrees; }
};

int main() {
    Temperature today(20.0);
    Fahrenheit report = today;
    cout << report.value() << endl;
    return 0;
}
~~~
:::

::: notes
Output: 68

The constructor reads the Celsius value through operator double from topic 2: t * 9.0 converts t to double first.

Full program: cpp/fahrenheit_conversion.cpp
:::

<!-- Slide 32 -->

---

## Spot the Conversions

~~~cpp
void show(Fahrenheit f);
Fahrenheit forecast(Temperature t);

int main() {
    Temperature today(20.0);
    Fahrenheit a = today;
    Fahrenheit b;
    b = today;
    show(today);
    Fahrenheit c = forecast(today);
    return 0;
}

Fahrenheit forecast(Temperature t) { return t; }
~~~

::: notes
Ask how many times a Temperature becomes a Fahrenheit. Answer: four. The definition of show is omitted; it prints its argument.
:::

<!-- Slide 33 -->

---

## Four Places Conversion Happens

~~~cpp
int main() {
    Temperature today(20.0);
    Fahrenheit a = today;              // copy initialization
    Fahrenheit b;
    b = today;                         // assignment
    show(today);                       // passing to a function
    Fahrenheit c = forecast(today);
    return 0;
}

Fahrenheit forecast(Temperature t) {
    return t;                          // return
}
~~~

::: notes
None of these lines names the constructor; the compiler generates every call. Assignment builds a temporary Fahrenheit and then uses Fahrenheit's copy assignment from 08.01. Inside the constructor, t * 9.0 is a fifth, hidden conversion: Temperature to double.

Full program: cpp/four_places.cpp
:::

<!-- Slide 34 -->

---

## Why This One Is Safe

| Line | Unit stated? | Data lost? |
|---|---|---|
| `double reading = today;` | No | No |
| `Fahrenheit report = today;` | Yes, in the type | No |
| `int whole = today;` | No | Yes, the fraction |

- Implicit conversion is safe when the target type names the meaning and nothing is lost.

::: notes
This resolves topic 2's Celsius-or-Fahrenheit problem: that conversion targeted a bare double. The standard library applies the same test in std::chrono: seconds convert to milliseconds implicitly because nothing is lost, while milliseconds to seconds requires duration_cast.
:::

<!-- Slide 35 -->

## First-Class Objects

`Temperature` now works everywhere an `int` does.

| An `int` can be | `Temperature` can be, because of |
|---|---|
| Initialized and copied | Constructors and the copy constructor (04.02, 08.01) |
| Assigned | Copy assignment (08.01) |
| Passed and returned | Copying (08.01) |
| Used with operators | Operator overloading (07.01, 07.02) |
| Converted | Conversion operators and converting constructors (today) |

::: notes
A first-class object is a user-defined type that behaves like a built-in type. Conversions were the last missing piece.
:::

<!-- Slide 36 -->

---

## Summary

- One class becomes another through a converting constructor in the target or a conversion operator in the source; write only one.
- Conversions fire in copy initialization, assignment, argument passing, and return, with no call written.

::: notes

:::
